title: Autonomous lawn mower
summary: A ROS-based autonomous mower combining YOLOv8 perception, LiDAR mapping, localization, coverage planning, motion control, and safety checks; my work spanned perception and autonomy integration.
role: AI & perception lead · mapping, planning and autonomy integration
imageAlt: The team’s assembled lawn mower prototype.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: A robot mower needs to understand both the surface it can cut and the obstacles it must avoid. Our team developed an autonomous mower concept for elderly and mobility-limited users, combining a physical platform with a modular autonomy stack.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: I led AI perception development: preparing image data, training and evaluating YOLOv8 detection and segmentation models, and connecting perception outputs with the wider robotic system. My contribution also extended to LiDAR mapping, localization, coverage planning, motion control, and safety checks, working with the team to connect these parts of the autonomy stack. Lawn, boundary, and barrier masks supported cut/no-cut reasoning, while object detections identified obstacles.

sections.title: How the system fits together
sections.text: I worked with the team to combine vision with LiDAR mapping, localization, coverage planning, motion control, and safety checks. ROS nodes exchange perception and navigation information, while Gazebo and RViz support staged simulation and visualization. The project includes both ROS 1 and ROS 2 development artifacts; the documented final report describes the ROS 1 pipeline.

sections.title: Results and limits
sections.text: The recorded validation scores are 0.764 box mAP50 and 0.745 mask mAP50. The team earned an Honourable Mention at Engineering Design Day. Perception was used alongside independent safety checks; these validation scores do not measure the safety or field coverage of the complete robot.

sections.title: Perception, simulation and integration
sections.text: I prepared and labeled vision data in Roboflow and trained Ultralytics YOLOv8 detection and segmentation models with PyTorch. Python and OpenCV supported image processing and the ROS perception interfaces. I also contributed to connecting occupancy-grid mapping, sensor fusion, coverage planning, motion control and safety checks in the team’s ROS pipeline; Gazebo and RViz provided simulation and visualization. The repository contains ROS 1 Noetic and ROS 2 development artifacts, while the documented final pipeline uses ROS 1. The browser demonstration runs the exported ONNX segmentation model. The hardware architecture pairs a Jetson Nano with an Arduino Mega; individual model validation and simulation results are distinct from complete outdoor robot validation.

title: Miniature C-arm surgical simulator
summary: A SolidWorks and PLA-printed C-arm prototype using Arduino C++, AccelStepper, A4988 motor drivers, and Bluetooth-to-3D Slicer integration.

sections.title: The task
sections.text: The team designed a miniature C-arm simulator to explore positioning and movement associated with surgical imaging equipment.

sections.title: The system
sections.text: The prototype combined a SolidWorks mechanical design and PLA printed parts with geared stepper motors and Bluetooth orientation sensing. Embedded control connected sensing to mechanical motion.

sections.title: What it demonstrates
sections.text: The work shows integration across mechanical design, sensing, actuation, and firmware. It is a training-oriented motion prototype rather than an X-ray imaging system.

sections.title: Mechanical, embedded and visualization tools
sections.text: Our team modeled the C-arm and surgical table in SolidWorks and fabricated the mechanism using PLA 3D printing. An Arduino Uno ran Arduino C++ with AccelStepper to control converted 28BYJ-48 motors through A4988 stepper drivers. Pushbuttons commanded translation and rotation; software travel limits and a shared enable line controlled movement and idle power. We worked with Bluetooth orientation sensing and the PLUS Server / 3D Slicer visualization chain. The report also records sensor communication and virtual-motion failures during later testing, so this was an integration prototype with unresolved reliability issues.

title: Smart wheelchair navigation
summary: ROS 2 / Nav2 indoor robot navigation with LiDAR mapping, Python/OpenCV hazard detection, and pyzbar barcode arrival checks.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Indoor assistive navigation needs more than a path between coordinates. The robot must recognize hazards, work around furniture, and confirm that it has reached the intended room.

sections.title: What we built
sections.text: Our team used a Yahboom Pi5 mobile robot to map a physical mock home with LiDAR and explore room-to-room navigation. OpenCV modules detected red tape representing hazardous floor zones and used color and shape cues for furniture context. QR/barcode checks provided a separate arrival signal.

sections.title: Testing and iteration
sections.text: Detector recalibration improved previously unsuccessful hazard and furniture tests. Obstacle avoidance remained partially successful, and the prototype could stall at a checkpoint if no barcode appeared. These limitations make the next steps clear: stronger recovery behavior and more robust arrival handling.

sections.title: Mapping, perception and arrival checks
sections.text: We used the Yahboom Pi5 robot, LiDAR mapping and the ROS 2 / Nav2 navigation stack to explore movement through a physical mock home. My perception work used Python and OpenCV: HSV color segmentation identified red-tape hazard zones, while color and shape cues supplied furniture context. pyzbar supported barcode and QR-code recognition as a separate room-arrival check. Testing exposed both detector calibration problems and a navigation checkpoint that could stall when a barcode was missing; the project documents those limitations alongside the successful perception tests.

title: Neonatal phototherapy blanket
summary: A SolidWorks medical-device design study combining fiber-optic light delivery, LED-driver selection, thermal analysis, and optical power budgeting.
role: Medical and assistive devices project · MME 4470

sections.title: The design question
sections.text: How could a phototherapy blanket be designed with affordability and the realities of resource-constrained care in mind? The course project develops the requirements and engineering rationale for a proposed device.

sections.title: The work
sections.text: I translated the treatment and usability needs into engineering requirements, then compared concepts for delivering blue light across a flexible treatment surface. My selected layout separates the LED source and driver from the fiber-optic pad, aiming to keep heat-producing electronics away from the infant while distributing light through the blanket. I developed the SolidWorks assembly and considered how the optical fibers, enclosure, power supply and control electronics could fit together in a portable design.

sections.title: Power, light and thermal design
sections.text: I evaluated blue COB5730 LEDs with CN5711 constant-current drivers and PWM dimming, and used optical power budgeting and runtime calculations to relate the proposed source to the treatment area and battery capacity. Thermal analysis informed the separation of the LED engine from the patient-contacting pad. These calculations guided a proposed device architecture; the blanket was a design study, not a manufactured or clinically tested treatment device.

sections.title: Scope
sections.text: This is a student design study. It is not a clinically validated device, and the portfolio does not claim a treatment outcome.

sections.title: Design tools and proposed hardware
sections.text: This was a medical-device design study supported by SolidWorks CAD, requirements analysis, Quality Function Deployment and a weighted concept-selection matrix. The selected concept separated a blue-LED engine from a fiber-optic treatment pad to reduce direct heat exposure. The proposed electronics used COB5730 LEDs, CN5711 constant-current PWM drivers and an 18650 battery supply. Optical power budgeting, runtime calculations and thermal analysis informed the design. These components describe the proposed architecture and engineering analysis, rather than a clinically validated or manufactured device.

title: Gem-sorting rover — Scooper Bot 10001
summary: An ESP32-S3 rover combining Arduino C++, PID wheel control, encoder feedback, TCS34725 color sensing, and 3D-printed sorting mechanisms.
imageAlt: Our Scooper Bot team with the assembled gem-sorting rover.

sections.title: The challenge
sections.text: The course challenge called for a rover that could collect and sort colored gems, then return to base within a time and parts budget.

sections.title: The design
sections.text: Our team used a funnel and revolving-door sorter with a color sensor inside a light-isolated chamber. ESP32-S3 firmware, encoder feedback, and motor control supported rover movement, while a servo-operated pickup mechanism handled the gems.

sections.title: Results and limitations
sections.text: The report describes pickup and color-sorting success, with return-to-base behavior limited by IR-beacon localization. This made sensing reliability and recovery an important part of the final analysis.

sections.title: Mechanics, sensing and embedded control
sections.text: The rover combined SolidWorks-designed and 3D-printed pickup and sorting mechanisms with ESP32-S3 Arduino C++ firmware. The MSE2202 library supported motor control and encoder feedback; PID control addressed wheel positioning. A TCS34725 color sensor distinguished gems inside a light-isolated sorting chamber, with servo-actuated collection and sorting hardware. Infrared-beacon homing and wheel traction were practical limitations during testing. This was a team build spanning mechanical design, sensor integration and embedded control.

title: SMA actuation & tendon-driven finger
role: Biosignal processing, actuator circuits and prosthetic mechanism design

gallery.caption: The printed three-link finger used to test tendon-driven curling and passive return.
Printed components for the finger mechanism.
Breadboard driver used to control the heating and cooling of the bendable SMA actuator.

summary: I connected muscle-signal processing with shape-memory alloy (SMA) actuation and designed a SolidWorks, 3D-printed tendon-driven finger to explore prosthetic movement.

sections.title: Project objective and design context
sections.text: I wanted to connect a muscle-control signal to a mechanism that could reproduce finger movement. Building on my earlier surface electromyography (sEMG) circuit, which measured electrical activity from forearm muscles, I explored how a compact actuator could generate tendon-like motion for prosthetic and wearable robotic devices. I designed a printed finger to test how a small tendon pull could create curling and return motion.

sections.title: How shape-memory alloy creates movement
sections.text: SMA stands for shape-memory alloy. I used thin nickel-titanium wire that contracts when heated by electrical current. Removing power lets it cool, while an opposing restoring force supports recovery. That contraction can pull a tendon like an artificial muscle. The small available movement and the time needed for heating and cooling shaped both the circuit and the mechanism design.

sections.title: Connecting muscle signals to actuation
sections.text: Working with my project partners, I built and tested a breadboard driver using a 555 timer oscillator, an IRLD024 MOSFET and a 1N4007 diode. Its on/off cycle gave the bendable SMA actuator time to heat and cool. I then connected the processed muscle signal from my earlier sEMG work: an INA126 instrumentation amplifier, high-pass and low-pass filters, and a precision rectifier. A forearm contraction raised the signal enough to switch current through the SMA actuator; relaxing the muscle removed the trigger.

sections.title: Designing the tendon-driven mechanism
sections.text: I modelled the three-link finger in SolidWorks, exported an STL file and fabricated the part by 3D printing. Its three segments represent the bones of an index finger, with thinner flexure regions at the joints and a tendon routed along the bending side. Pulling the tendon curled the finger; releasing it let the printed flexures restore a straighter shape. I used this mechanism to test how a small pull could produce useful joint motion.

sections.title: What I demonstrated
sections.text: I tested the electrical SMA actuator and the printed finger as separate parts of the project. In the finger video, I pull the tendon manually to simulate SMA contraction. The muscle-triggered bendable SMA actuator was tested separately. Together, the work connected biosignal conditioning, thermal actuator control and prosthetic mechanism design, and showed how cooling time and limited actuator travel constrain movement.

title: Liquid crystal elastomer soft actuators
summary: Experimental research on liquid crystal elastomers for soft robotics, from material preparation and fabrication to heat-responsive motion, load testing, and a solar-tracker demonstrator.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: During my internship at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), I worked on liquid crystal elastomers for responsive soft actuators. The project explored how a flexible polymer could produce useful motion when exposed to heat or light. The broader research direction brought together the actuator material, printed heating elements, and sensing; my experimental work focused on preparing the material, shaping it, and understanding its response.

sections.title: Fabrication and preparation
sections.text: I worked with cast LCE formulations and direct-ink-writing approaches, preparing mixtures and carrying samples through molding, stretching, and curing. I also developed sketches for laser cutting and worked with LCE elements attached to flexible silicone substrates. The fabrication work involved adjusting preparation and printing conditions, then checking whether the resulting material could be handled and tested as an actuator.

sections.title: Actuation and application tests
sections.text: I tested how the LCE strips contracted and recovered under heating and cooling, including experiments with suspended weights to see whether the material could perform mechanical work. I also tested LCE elements in a solar-tracker demonstrator, where heating one side changed the orientation of the supported solar cell. These experiments connected the behavior of the material to a possible device application.

sections.title: Thermal response and coatings
sections.text: I investigated conductive layers and light-absorbing treatments as ways to alter the thermal response. I compared coated and uncoated strips, tracked their heating and cooling behavior, and recorded changes in shape and length under heat and sunlight. The observations helped distinguish contraction, bending, and recovery, while identifying which coating and fabrication choices needed further testing.

sections.title: Fabrication and characterization methods
sections.text: My experimental work combined polymer preparation and casting with syringe-based direct ink writing, laser-cut sample preparation and heat-responsive actuation tests. I investigated how material preparation and fabrication affected movement, tested load lifting, and contributed to a solar-cell demonstrator. The report records iterative material and fabrication work; proposed integrated sensing and heater concepts are separate from the experimental demonstrations shown here.

title: Household energy forecasting
summary: TensorFlow/Keras LSTM forecasting of household electricity use, with pandas/NumPy preprocessing, engineered energy features, and time-series windowing.
role: Group project · preprocessing, features, and LSTM development

metrics.label: Reported test MAE · report target scale

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Minute-level electricity measurements contain temporal structure, missing values, and relationships between aggregate and sub-metered consumption. A useful model needs careful data preparation as well as a suitable architecture.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: I worked on preprocessing, Power Factor and Global Active Energy features, and the LSTM architecture and tuning. The final group model used two 128-unit LSTM layers with a dense prediction head and a 256-step input window.

sections.title: Results in context
sections.text: The report records a final test R² of 0.65 and MAE of 1.07 on the project’s target scale. Earlier model attempts performed poorly, making iterative diagnosis a central part of the work. Related assignments compared ARIMA, MLP, CNN, RNN, LSTM, GRU, TCN, and Transformer-based approaches across separate datasets.

sections.title: Data preparation and sequence-model development
sections.text: I worked on preprocessing and engineered features for the group’s household electricity forecasting project. pandas and NumPy supported time-indexed data preparation and calculations such as power factor and global active energy. TensorFlow / Keras implemented sliding-window LSTM models with Dense layers and dropout, trained in Google Colab. We iterated on window length and network structure, then compared predictions and training/validation behavior using MSE, MAE and R-squared. scikit-learn supported the surrounding preprocessing and evaluation workflow.

title: Machine-learning fairness and differential privacy
summary: Python coursework using AIF360, fairlearn, DoWhy, diffprivlib, TensorFlow, and scikit-learn to investigate fairness, causality, and privacy tradeoffs.
role: Individual fairness, causality and privacy investigations

sections.title: The question
sections.text: A model can perform well on average while producing different error patterns across groups. Removing a sensitive feature alone does not remove information carried by correlated features.

sections.title: Fairness and privacy investigations
sections.text: I examined classification disparities in COMPAS data, explored fairness interventions, built causal-analysis exercises, and tested differentially private regression models. These investigations connect evaluation choices with explicit assumptions about fairness and privacy.

sections.title: Libraries and analysis workflow
sections.text: I used pandas / NumPy and scikit-learn for data preparation, classification and evaluation, with Matplotlib for result plots. AIF360 and fairlearn supported group-fairness metrics and mitigation experiments, including Exponentiated Gradient Reduction and adversarial debiasing with TensorFlow. DoWhy supported causal modeling and refutation checks. In the privacy work, diffprivlib linear and logistic regression models were compared with scikit-learn baselines across privacy-budget settings. These were modeling investigations of tradeoffs, rather than a deployed decision system.

title: Six-axis robot arm kinematics and path planning
eyebrow: Six-axis robot arm kinematics and path planning
summary: MATLAB kinematics and potential-field motion planning for a six-axis manipulator, using DH parameters, Jacobians, and obstacle-avoidance parameter sweeps.

sections.title: Full-path simulation
sections.text: I implemented and tested the manipulator’s planned trajectory in simulation. The recorded demonstration shows the six-axis arm completing the full path, bringing the kinematic model and trajectory planning together in motion.

sections.title: The task
sections.text: We modeled a six-degree-of-freedom CrustCrawler arm for a bin-picking application, then planned end-effector motion around obstacles in the workspace.

sections.title: The implementation
sections.text: The project includes Denavit–Hartenberg forward kinematics, geometric inverse kinematics, Jacobian calculations, and potential-field planning. Parameter sweeps investigated stability and path smoothness.

sections.title: Limits and related work
sections.text: Representative planned paths avoided modeled spherical obstacles. The point-mass approximation and local minima limit what the simulation establishes. Related Baxter work explored PID and computed-torque control on a seven-axis robot.

sections.title: Analytical modeling and planner implementation
sections.text: We developed a MATLAB kinematic model for a six-axis serial manipulator, using Denavit–Hartenberg parameters, forward and inverse kinematics, and Jacobian calculations. The potential-field planner combined attraction toward the target with repulsion from spherical obstacles; a Jacobian-transpose mapping converted Cartesian motion into joint updates. Parameter sweeps examined path curvature, obstacle influence and convergence across representative tasks. Simulink formed part of the broader manipulator modeling and control coursework; the figures on this page document the kinematic and planning study.

title: Cardiovascular modeling & cardiac-device simulations
role: Cardiovascular simulation and analysis · team project contributions

gallery.caption: Total modeled flow versus LVAD flow for resting and exercising conditions; the marked bends indicate where pump flow begins to dominate.

summary: I used MATLAB to investigate two cardiac-device questions: how LVAD support changes circulation, and how biphasic shock timing changes modeled cardiac membrane response.

sections.title: Two cardiac-device questions
sections.text: I investigated cardiovascular support and cardiac electrical stimulation through two related MATLAB studies. The LVAD work examined blood flow, ventricular loading and pump control. The defibrillation work examined source waveforms and cardiac membrane voltage. They share a modeling and parameter-analysis approach, with separate physiological models and results.

sections.title: LVAD · The question
sections.text: A left ventricular assist device supplies flow alongside a weakened heart, but stronger pump support also changes the pressures and workload of the native ventricle. Our study examined this interaction under resting and exercise conditions using a simplified cardiovascular model.

sections.title: LVAD · Comparing assisted and unassisted circulation
sections.text: We varied the pump contribution and compared total systemic flow, ventricular pressure-volume loops, and ventricular and arterial pressure traces. The outputs show how increasing support can unload the ventricle until the pump supplies nearly all of the flow. Comparing the pressure traces with and without assistance helped explain when the aortic valve could open and why pulsatility changed.

sections.title: LVAD · Physiologically responsive control
sections.text: We then overlaid a Starling-like supervisory control law on the relationship between pump flow and end-diastolic pressure. The aim was to select a resting operating point and examine how that same controller responded to the increased demand represented by the exercise model, while retaining a contribution from the native heart.

sections.title: LVAD · Interpreting the model
sections.text: The report compares the model’s baseline filling-pressure behavior with a reference example and discusses the consequences of that mismatch. The investigation treats the outputs as simulation results: the simplified circulation, fixed parameters, and limited physiological feedback restrict how far the controller findings can be generalized.

sections.title: LVAD · Simulation and physiological interpretation
sections.text: I used MATLAB scripts to investigate ventricular assistance by varying pump flow and comparing pressure, flow and ventricular-volume waveforms. The supplied cardiovascular model uses a Windkessel representation and time-varying ventricular elastance. Batch runs and pressure–volume analysis helped explain how increasing LVAD support changes the ventricle’s contribution to circulation. A subsequent control investigation related pump flow to end-diastolic pressure, keeping the model’s simplifications and validation limits explicit.

sections.title: Defibrillation · Waveform timing and membrane response
sections.text: The investigation compared two ways of defining a biphasic exponential waveform: ending each phase at a specified voltage tilt, or choosing its duration directly. A cardiac-cell electrical model connected the applied source waveform with the resulting membrane-voltage response.

sections.title: Defibrillation · What we investigated
sections.text: We examined the source time constant and energy-storage assumptions, swept the membrane time constant, and compared the membrane response at the end of each phase. The first phase was assessed for depolarization and the second for the residual membrane response after the polarity reversal.

sections.title: Defibrillation · Matching the two parameterizations
sections.text: The final comparison converted chosen phase durations into their corresponding tilt values and ran both formulations with the same source assumptions. The resulting membrane-voltage curves nearly coincide, illustrating that matched fixed-tilt and tuned-duration settings can describe the same underlying exponential waveform.

sections.title: Defibrillation · Project scope
sections.text: The deliverables were MATLAB calculations, waveform overlays, and a written interpretation of the electrical model. These are educational simulation results rather than device testing or clinical validation.

sections.title: Defibrillation · Waveform construction and response analysis
sections.text: The MATLAB study constructed biphasic exponential source waveforms and examined their modeled cardiac-cell membrane response. I investigated waveform tilt, phase duration and timing, using response plots and parameter comparisons to explain how a change at the source altered membrane voltage. The report figures distinguish the applied shock waveform from the modeled membrane response; the analysis does not establish a clinical defibrillation protocol.

sections.text: I worked on robot CAD parts, assembly, and fabrication. The work connected mechanical designs with printed parts and servo-actuated mechanisms, including the robot components shown here.

sections.title: Computer vision and speech interfaces
sections.text: My internship projects included computer-vision exercises and a speech-to-text web interface. These tasks connected camera or microphone input with software that presents the result to a user.

sections.title: Web development and integration
sections.text: I also worked on web interfaces and API integration across internship tasks. The projects combined mechanical, electronics, AI, and software work within one engineering internship.

sections.title: Mechanical and software internship work
sections.text: My internship work covered SolidWorks robot-component design, STL preparation, 3D printing, servo mechanisms and control-circuit prototyping. The software work included Python / OpenCV vision interfaces, JavaScript web interfaces and a speech-to-text prototype. The page combines the original fabrication, simulation and interface material from these activities. Supplied training decks and upstream example packages are reference material, so their complete technology stacks are not presented as tools I independently implemented.
